title: Core memory reborn as vortex-chirality nanorings threaded by crosspoint lines
idea: Shrink the 1950s ferrite core to a 40-nm CoFeB/NiFe nanoring whose bit is the clockwise/counter-clockwise flux-closure vortex, exactly the core's circumferential flux. Write by coincident half-currents in an X and a Y line threading the ring hole (the core's square-loop half-select), and read non-destructively through a small MTJ patch on one ring segment instead of the core's destructive sense wire.
why: Removes capacitor and access transistor (Facts 1, 3); flux closure has no stray field so rings pack at ~4F2 and stack in decks; zero refresh and ~zero standby; claims 2-3x density per area at equal F with 4 decks.

title: Bell Labs 1952 ferroelectric matrix revived with square-loop HZO superlattices
idea: The first ferroelectric memories (BaTiO3 crystal matrices, 1952) were transistor-free passive crosspoints that died of half-select disturb because their loops were not square. Revive the passive matrix with nucleation-limited HfZrO/ZrO2 superlattices whose Al2O3 pinning planes make switching probability at V/3 <1e-12 per pulse while full V switches in 10 ns, stacking 8 passive decks in BEOL.
why: No access device and 8 decks give ~4F2/8 effective cell, ~5-10x bits per mask (Facts 2, 4); non-volatile so no refresh (Fact 3); still destructive read with write-back.

title: Williams tube 2.0: on-chip field-emitter arrays writing a charge mosaic
idea: Like the Williams-Kilburn CRT that stored bits as charge spots on a phosphor face, a vacuum-sealed micro-cavity holds a carbon-nanotube field-emitter array, each emitter electrostatically deflected over a 4x4 um patch of a nitride charge-trap mosaic. Bits are 20-nm trapped-charge spots written by beam dose and read by secondary-electron yield on re-scan, with write-back exactly like the Williams regeneration raster.
why: No wire, transistor or capacitor per bit: periphery is per-emitter not per-row (Fact 7) and bits are not litho-defined (Fact 4); ~40k bits per emitter gives ~5 Gb/cm2 per layer from old-node litho; beam slew ~20-50 ns.

title: Selectron revival: secondary-emission bistable islands held by a flood beam
idea: RCA's 1948 Selectron kept each bit static because a floating eyelet sat at either cathode or collector potential, self-reinforced by secondary-emission yield above or below 1 under a holding flood. Build a nano-vacuum layer over an array of 30-nm floating metal islands with an on-chip planar flood emitter; islands are bistable at two potentials, written by pulsed X/Y control gates and read capacitively through a buried sense electrode.
why: Static, refresh-free charge storage with no transistor leakage tail (Fact 3) and no capacitor (Fact 1); standby cost is one flood current shared by millions of bits (~pA-class per bit).

title: Plasma-panel wall-charge memory shrunk to sealed field-emission nanogaps
idea: AC plasma displays (PLATO, 1964) had inherent memory: wall charge left on the dielectric keeps a fired cell firing under a common sustain wave while unfired cells stay dark. Replace the gas discharge with field emission across 20-nm sealed dielectric-coated nanogaps; a global sustain AC re-deposits wall charge each half-cycle only in 'on' cells, and X/Y address pulses add or erase wall charge.
why: The hysteresis itself is the selector, so the crosspoint is 4F2 and stackable; the global sustain is built-in refresh with no row activations, which also removes row hammer (Facts 3, 8, 9).

title: Ferreed crosspoint revived: nanomagnet-latched NEMS contact as the bit
idea: Bell's 1960 ferreed latched a reed contact with a remanent magnet. Shrink it to a 100-nm NEMS cantilever with a CoPt hard-magnet tip that latches onto a soft-magnetic pad when the pad is magnetized parallel and springs open when antiparallel; a current-strap pulse flips the pad to write, and contact conduction (on/off >1e8) reads.
why: Bit held magnetically (non-volatile, no refresh, Fact 3) while the readout is a mechanical switch with near-infinite on/off ratio, so it self-selects in a crosspoint with no transistor or selector (Facts 2, 7); aJ-class read.

title: Bobeck bubble chip reborn: skyrmion minor loops with replicate gates
idea: Bring back the bubble chip's major/minor-loop organization (many short minor loops, transfer gates into a major loop) using 20-nm skyrmions in compensated ferrimagnetic GdFeCo stepped by spin-orbit-torque pulses. Keep the bubble chip's replicate gate, which splits a skyrmion and sends the copy to the detector, so reads are non-destructive.
why: At 40-nm pitch and ~1 bit/ns stepping a 32-bit minor loop gives <=32 ns access; only tracks are patterned so ~2F2 per bit, no capacitor or transistor per bit (Facts 1-4), non-volatile.

title: Vertical Bloch line memory revived with DMI-tuned stripe domains
idea: NEC's 1983 VBL memory stored bits as pairs of vertical Bloch lines inside the walls of stripe domains, features far smaller than bubbles. Revive it in [Pt/Co/Ir] multilayers whose interfacial DMI is tuned near the Neel-Bloch crossover so Bloch-line pairs are stable at ~10-nm pitch, shifted along walls by in-plane current pulses and read where the wall end meets an MTJ.
why: Bits defined by topology, not litho: ~10x skyrmion-track density potential (Tb/in2 class) with no transistor or capacitor per bit (Facts 1, 2, 4).

title: Twistor reborn: helical-anisotropy nanowires read by Wiedemann torsion pulses
idea: Bell's twistor wound magnetic tape helically on a copper wire. Electroplate vertical Cu-core/CoFe-shell nanowires under applied torsion so the shell has a helical easy axis, write helical domain segments by coincident axial current plus a tier strap, and read by the Wiedemann effect: a core current pulse twists each domain, launching a torsional acoustic echo sensed by an AlN piezo pad at the wire top.
why: A vertical wire is a 3D string with no transistor per tier (Fact 2); a mechanical readout signal sidesteps resistance-variation tails; ~64 bits per 20-nm wire.

title: Plated-wire memory rebuilt as vertical plated vias in 3D stacks
idea: Plated-wire memory (Voyager era) stored bits in the circumferential magnetization of permalloy plated on a wire and read them non-destructively by tilting it with a word strap. Make the wire a vertical copper pillar in a 3D-NAND-style hole lined with circumferentially anisotropic CoFeB, use the stacked tier planes as word straps, write by coincident pillar plus strap current, and read by a small strap pulse that tilts the film and induces a pillar voltage.
why: 100+ tiers from one hole etch with no lateral transistor or capacitor (Fact 2), non-destructive read (Fact 8), non-volatile (Fact 3); ~1/5 the cost per bit of 2D DRAM if signal suffices.

title: Atanasoff capacitor drum as transistorless capacitors swept by MEMS brushes
idea: The 1942 ABC stored bits on capacitors mounted on a rotating drum, read and regenerated by brushes, with no switch per capacitor. Fabricate a field of isolated nano-capacitors (10-nm dielectric, no junction, no transistor) under a 2D MEMS array of conductive probe tips, each tip scanning a 50x50 um field with its own sense amp.
why: Without an access transistor leakage is dielectric tunneling only, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours (Fact 3 refresh ~0); ~2F2 cells with no wordline; microsecond 'drum tier' that needs a DRAM cache.

title: Vertical CCD charge columns: 3D DRAM without per-tier transistors
idea: Revive 1970s serial CCD memory vertically: the tier word planes of a 3D stack act as CCD transfer phases around a vertical crystalline-Si or IGZO channel, so charge packets march up the column to one sense/regenerate node at the top. Three tiers per bit and 240 tiers give 80 bits per column.
why: Removes the lateral transistor and capacitor that block 3D DRAM (Fact 2) with 3D-NAND-style one-etch tiers; full column shift at ~1 ns/step gives ~80 ns access; ~10x bits per area.

title: Goto parametron revived as phase-bistable NEMS resonator bits
idea: Goto's 1954 parametron stored a bit as the 0 or pi phase of an oscillator pumped at twice its frequency. Use arrays of ~1 GHz AlScN or SiN NEMS beams pumped by a shared 2 GHz line; a bit is the vibration phase, written by a small seed pulse, read by phase-sensitive piezo detection, and majority-voted in place.
why: Holding set by mechanical Q, not junction leakage, so no leakage tail (Fact 3); a shared pump replaces per-row refresh; in-place majority logic trims data movement (Fact 5); needs <1 fW pump per bit.

title: Crowe-cell persistent-current loops with nanocryotron readout for cryogenic AI
idea: The 1957 Crowe cell stored bits as clockwise or counter-clockwise supercurrent in a thin-film loop. Build it from 100-nm NbN kinetic-inductance loops read by the nTron (the modern three-terminal cryotron), stacked with cryo-CMOS or SFQ accelerators in dedicated AI pods.
why: Zero static dissipation, zero refresh, ~1e-19 J switching (Facts 3, 10); only pays at pod scale after ~400 W/W 4 K cooling overhead; target 10x system energy per bit including cooling.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode latch reborn as one transistor plus broken-gap diodes
idea: 1960s fast registers used series tunnel-diode pairs (Goto pairs) as bistable stores. Stack two InAs/GaSb broken-gap tunnel diodes (peak ~1 uA, valley ~1 pA through an engineered barrier) on the storage node of one access transistor so negative differential resistance holds two stable voltages without refresh.
why: Static retention in ~8F2 removes refresh (Fact 3) and the capacitor (Fact 1); standby is valley current, ~1 pW per bit (~1 mW per Gb).

title: Spin-echo storage revived: electron-spin ensembles as phase-coded bit trains
idea: In 1955 Anderson and Fernbach proposed computer memories that store data in spin precession phases and recall them with a refocusing pulse. Couple ensembles of donor electron spins in isotopically pure 28Si:P to on-chip microwave resonators so each resonator holds a train of thousands of time-multiplexed, phase-encoded bits recalled as echoes.
why: No transistor or capacitor per bit and time multiplexing puts thousands of bits on one resonator; spin coherence of seconds dwarfs 64 ms; needs cryogenic operation, so speculative.

title: 1960s holographic memory revived on thin-film lithium niobate photonics
idea: RCA and Bell holographic stores wrote whole pages as interference gratings in photorefractive crystals. Put an Fe-doped thin-film LN slab under a SiN optical phased array that steers the reference angle electro-optically in ns, storing ~1000 angle-multiplexed 4-kb pages in a 100x100 um slab read in parallel onto a Ge photodiode row.
why: Volume storage escapes planar litho density (Fact 4) and a page read uses the overfetch instead of wasting it for streamed weights (Fact 8); thermal fixing for retention; target 10 Gb/cm2 equivalent with no transistor per bit.

title: Persistent spectral hole burning: a thousand frequency bits per spot
idea: IBM's 1978 PHB patent stored bits as narrow holes burned at chosen frequencies in an inhomogeneously broadened absorption line. Use room-temperature PHB films (Sm2+ in BaFCl-type hosts) where each diffraction-limited spot holds ~1000 frequency channels, written and read by a fast chirped laser and photodiode.
why: Frequency becomes a third storage dimension (~1000x bits per spot) without lithography (Fact 4); erase endurance and speed unproven, so a speculative capacity tier.

title: Zuse Z1 sliding-plate memory as nanomechanical detented shuttles
idea: Zuse's 1938 Z1 held bits as the position of sliding metal plates with pins. Fabricate 200-nm Si or TiN shuttles in BEOL cavities with a buckled-beam double-well detent, set left or right by an electrostatic comb pulse and read by differential capacitance to a sense line.
why: Bit is a mechanical position: non-volatile, zero leakage, contact-free so effectively unlimited endurance (Fact 3); ~10 ns switching at this size; ~20F2 cell but zero refresh energy.

title: Dekatron glow-stepping counter revived as a multi-position domain-wall cell
idea: The Dekatron stored a decimal digit as the position of one glow among ten cathodes. Store 4 bits as the position of a single domain wall among 16 notches in a 400-nm magnetic strip, stepped by current pulses and read by an MTJ whose free layer overlaps a wedge so resistance tracks wall position.
why: 4 bits per cell instead of 1 gives density without a litho shrink (Fact 4), non-volatile with no capacitor (Facts 1, 3); risk is separating 16 resistance levels.

title: Gunn-domain delay line: travelling field domains as a shift register
idea: 1960s engineers proposed Gunn-effect domains as high-speed memories. Launch bits as high-field domains travelling ~1e5 m/s along a long n-GaN or GaAs channel, recirculate them through a regenerating trigger electrode, and tap them with capacitive pickups along the channel.
why: ~1-um bit spacing at 100 Gb/s per channel and ~10 ns per mm tap latency with no cell structure at all; domain stability at sub-um scale is very uncertain.

title: 1950s diode-capacitor store reborn as stacked selector-capacitor crosspoint decks
idea: Early machines held bits on capacitors gated by diodes rather than transistors. Revive it as 1S1C: planar MIM capacitors stacked with a two-terminal ovonic or punch-through selector (~1e-15 A off) in BEOL decks, accessed by V/2-biased crosspoint lines with short 64-cell bitline segments so ~0.5 fF suffices.
why: No lateral transistor and no high-AR pillar (Facts 1, 2): 4F2 per deck x 4 decks in BEOL; refresh interval set by selector leakage rather than junction tails.

title: Revival tournament: twelve forgotten storage elements on one common test chip
idea: Fund 12 revived storage elements (core, plated wire, bubble, parametron, CCD, Selectron and others) to a shared 1-Mb test vehicle with identical sense/IO periphery and one scorecard (fJ/bit, ns, F2, retention, endurance) on shared shuttle wafers, with kill-or-scale gates at 6 and 12 months and prize money for crossing DRAM-class thresholds.
why: Compares physics fairly at ~$2M per element instead of $100M+ per startup and compresses discovery time; attacks the capital and time chokepoints.

title: CCD-era pinned storage well as a DRAM cell in image-sensor fabs
idea: Interline CCDs and the 1980 pinned photodiode held charge in fully depleted, surface-pinned buried wells with dark current near 1 e-/s. Use existing 65/45-nm CMOS-image-sensor flows (pinned well, transfer gate, floating diffusion, source follower) to store a bit as ~1000 electrons in a contactless pinned well, read by transfer to a shared floating diffusion with in-cell gain.
why: Retention of seconds to minutes instead of 64 ms (Fact 3: ~100x less refresh) and gain readout sidesteps the capacitor wall (Fact 1); CIS fabs are mature, EUV-free, with idle capacity; ~10x less dense than DRAM, so a refresh-free tier.

title: Intel 1103 three-transistor cell rebuilt on 22-nm FD-SOI back gates
idea: The first commercial DRAM (1103, 1970) was a 3T gain cell. Rebuild it on existing 22/28-nm FD-SOI lines with a thick-oxide write transistor held under reverse back-bias for sub-aA leakage and a thin-oxide read transistor whose back gate is pulsed only during reads for ~5x read current.
why: No capacitor (Fact 1); back-bias pushes retention to ~1 s (Fact 3: refresh energy down ~10-15x); non-destructive read removes write-back (Fact 8); existing non-EUV capacity.

title: Transfluxor multi-aperture micro-yokes made in hard-disk head wafer fabs
idea: RCA's 1956 transfluxor used a two-aperture core whose main-leg flux state blocks or unblocks flux around the small aperture, giving non-destructive reads. HDD write-head fabs already plate NiFe/CoFe yokes around Cu coils at 0.1-1 um; build micro-transfluxors there whose minor-aperture coil reads by an AC drive that couples only when the main leg is unblocked.
why: Non-destructive, non-volatile, radiation-hard storage with no transistor per bit on existing head-wafer capacity (including U.S. sites); ~1 um2 cells, so it targets rad-hard and edge markets that now consume DRAM plus flash.

title: Apollo core-rope ROM reborn as via-coupled multi-layer weight store
idea: Apollo's rope memory encoded bits as whether a sense wire threaded a core. Encode frozen AI weights as presence or absence of via stubs coupling word lines to sense lines across 8 metal-layer pairs of an existing 40-nm logic process (one custom via mask per layer); pulsing a word line induces charge only on sense lines with a stub, so there is no DC sneak path.
why: Frees DRAM/HBM now spent on immutable weights; no refresh, no capacitor; 8 planes x 4F2 at 40 nm is ~800 nm2 per bit, about DRAM's 864 nm2, at far lower capex and no EUV.

title: MNOS revival: direct-tunnel nitride-trap one-transistor cell on SONOS lines
idea: The 1967 MNOS stored charge in nitride traps behind a thin oxide. On existing 40/28-nm embedded SONOS lines, thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5 nm so writes are pure direct tunneling at +-3 V in ~20 ns, giving hour-scale retention ('dynamic flash') without hot-carrier or FN damage.
why: 1T cell with no capacitor (Fact 1), refresh every ~10 minutes instead of 64 ms (Fact 3: ~10,000x fewer refreshes), non-destructive read; endurance projected 1e12+ because direct tunneling avoids oxide wear, still to be proven DRAM-class.

title: T-RAM thyristor latch revived on existing SOI production lines
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor's thin capacitively-coupled thyristor (abandoned around 2010) held bits as the latched state of a gate-coupled pnpn device. Re-target it to existing 22FDX and 45-nm PD-SOI flows, using modern back-bias to cut standby current and ALD gate dielectric to tighten the coupled gate.
why: Regenerative bistable storage in ~10F2 with ~1 ns reads and large read current, no capacitor (Fact 1), and only pulse-refresh every few seconds (Fact 3); entirely existing SOI capacity.

title: Widrow memistor reborn as a protonic WO3 three-terminal BEOL gain cell
idea: Widrow's 1960 memistor stored a value as electroplated copper thickness on a resistive film read through separate terminals. Build a three-terminal protonic cell (WO3 channel, ZrO2:H electrolyte, Pd gate) in the BEOL of an existing 180/130-nm fab; write pulses move H+ in or out and the channel conductance is read without disturbing it.
why: Separated read path means no read disturb (Fact 8), hour retention (Fact 3), fJ writes below 1 V (Fact 10); ~1e9 endurance makes it a weight/state tier rather than general DRAM; BEOL-only on U.S. 200-mm fabs.

title: Contiguous-disk bubble tracks driven by one global rotating field
idea: Late-1980s bubble chips used ion-implanted contiguous-disk tracks that moved sub-lithographic bubbles under a global rotating in-plane field. On existing 200-mm lines, deposit perpendicular CoTb films, define tracks by ion implantation through a 0.5-um mask (no magnetic etch), drive every track at once with a package-level rotating-field coil, and detect with same-fab magnetoresistive bridges.
why: Bit size set by material (~100 nm) not litho; per-track drivers vanish so periphery shrinks (Fact 7); non-volatile; ~us latency at 10 MHz field makes a capacity tier that offloads DRAM.

title: Magnetostrictive delay line reborn as recirculating spin-wave registers
idea: 1950s calculators stored bits as acoustic pulses in magnetostrictive nickel wire. Store bits instead as ~5 GHz spin-wave packets in permalloy/CoFeB waveguide loops patterned on an existing 180-nm line, with inductive antennas and a CMOS amplifier regenerating each loop every pass.
why: Bit is a wave in flight: no cell, no capacitor; ~1-um bit spacing gives ~0.1-1 Mb/mm2 and 10-50 ns latency in short loops for FIFO/KV-cache streaming buffers; regeneration energy is the open risk.

title: Relay-computer revival: NEM pull-in hysteresis latch at zero current
idea: Relay and neon-lamp memories held bits inside a hysteresis window between pick-up and drop-out. In existing MEMS foundries or 180-nm BEOL, build TiN or poly-Si cantilever relays biased between their pull-out (~1.5 V) and pull-in (~3 V) voltages, so a pulled-in beam stays in and a released beam stays out at zero DC current.
why: Static storage with zero leakage through an air gap (Fact 3), abrupt selector-like on/off, no capacitor; ~1 um2 cells make a low-power state store built entirely in existing MEMS capacity.

title: Mercury delay line reborn in RF SAW-filter fabs on lithium tantalate
idea: The UNIVAC mercury tank stored bits as acoustic pulses circulating between transducers. Existing RF front-end filter fabs (LiTaO3/LiNbO3, 0.25-0.5 um litho, billions of units per year, some in the U.S.) can make folded SAW delay loops with interdigital transducers, paired with a CMOS regenerator die.
why: No cell structure; ~4 km/s acoustic velocity gives 50,000x more delay per mm than light, so 2 GHz x 1 us loops hold 2 kb each as a refresh-free streaming tier that offloads sequential DRAM traffic; value is capex and supply chain, not density.

title: Williams-tube logic: a flat-panel display fab used as a memory fab
idea: The Williams tube turned a display into memory; do the same with existing Gen-8.5 IGZO TFT display fabs, where every pixel is already a 1T1C charge cell. Pattern dense 1.5-um-rule TFT memory arrays (no liquid crystal, no light) on glass, tile them with TFT sense amps, and cut them into memory sheets.
why: Glass avoids CZ silicon and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles; ~66 kb/mm2 x 5.5 m2 is ~45 GB per sheet at roughly $10/GB on idle display capacity, parity in a shortage; us-class latency means a CXL capacity tier.

title: Ramtron FeRAM revived with non-destructive piezoelectric-sign readout
idea: Early 1T1C PZT FeRAM suffered destructive reads and fatigue. On existing 130-nm FRAM lines that already integrate PZT, read polarization by applying a small AC voltage and sensing the sign of the resulting piezoelectric strain with a capacitive or piezoresistive sense layer over the capacitor, as piezoresponse microscopy does.
why: Removes destructive read and write-back (Fact 8: ~50% read energy) and the fatigue cycles they cause; non-volatile (Fact 3); existing FRAM capacity.

title: Drum memory reborn: stationary disk media scanned by head arrays
idea: Drum memories held bits on a moving magnetic surface under fixed heads. Invert it: existing HDD media sputter lines coat granular CoCrPt on Si, and existing HDD head fabs build 1000-head arrays on a MEMS x-y stage (+-50 um), each head owning a micro-field of media.
why: ~1 Tb/in2 media density with no lithography per bit; us access and massive parallel bandwidth make a DRAM-offload capacity tier (cold KV caches, embeddings) built on under-used HDD capacity.

title: EDSAC-style delay loops rebuilt as WDM light on photonics foundries
idea: Recirculate bits as light in low-loss SiN spiral loops on existing 45/90-nm silicon-photonics foundry lines (such as AIM Photonics), with 32 WDM channels at 50 Gb/s and an SOA plus clock-recovery regenerator per loop.
why: 1.6 Tb/s x 20 ns loop holds 32 kb with <=20 ns latency: DRAM-class access, no cells, and optical I/O straight to accelerators (Fact 5); energy per regeneration pass is the risk.

title: Core-plane separation: universal 28-nm periphery die bonded to revived arrays
idea: Core memories separated the passive core plane from shared drive and sense electronics. Split every revived storage array (magnetic, mechanical, charge) from a standard 28-nm sense/IO die hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer on existing CIS-fab bonding lines, with a programmable sense front end (current, voltage, inductive, phase).
why: Periphery is ~49% of DRAM die (Fact 7); moving it to a cheap mature-node die makes arrays ~100% array and lets any exotic element reach a DDR/CXL interface without its own PHY.

title: Drum optimum-programming compiler for in-flight delay-line memories
idea: 1950s drum programmers (SOAP for the IBM 650) placed each word where it would pass under the head just in time. Build a compiler and runtime that schedules AI tensor tiles into recirculating loops (acoustic, photonic, spin-wave) so each tile reaches its tap exactly when the accelerator needs it.
why: Turns circulation delay into near-zero effective latency for predictable AI dataflows (weights, KV streams), so cheap delay storage displaces DRAM capacity with no fab at all.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor memory: pseudocapacitive planar cell beats the pillar wall
idea: Early electrolytic storage used electrochemical double layers for enormous capacitance. Deposit ALD hydrous RuO2 or MnO2 with a solid proton-conducting electrolyte as a planar storage capacitor on an existing 65/90-nm logic flow, reaching ~5 fF in ~0.05 um2 with no high-aspect-ratio etch.
why: Attacks the charge wall (Fact 1) with ~100x capacitance density and skips the 60:1 pillar etch (Fact 4 capex); risks are ns-scale ion response and self-discharge.

title: Magnetostriction reused: piezo-strain-written nanomagnets on FRAM PZT lines
idea: The magnetostriction behind 1950s delay lines can write bits: place elliptical Galfenol or Terfenol-D nanomagnets on a PZT film using existing 130-nm FRAM PZT tooling, flip them with a voltage-driven strain pulse plus small bias field, and read with an AMR/GMR stack sputtered in the same BEOL.
why: aJ-class current-free writes break the CV2 floor (Fact 10), non-volatile (Fact 3), no capacitor (Fact 1); uses existing PZT and magnetic sputter tools.

title: Plated-wire space heritage: sell rad-hard magnetic memory first, then scale
idea: Plated wire flew on Voyager and the Shuttle because radiation cannot upset it. Launch a revived plated-wire-style magnetic memory on existing U.S. 200-mm trailing-node fabs into space and defense, where rad-hard memory sells at ~1000x DRAM $/bit, and use the margin to fund density learning toward commodity parts.
why: Funds a new storage element without a $15B fab, builds U.S. manufacturing know-how, and de-risks the physics on paying customers.

title: Advance market commitment for element-agnostic trailing-node working memory
idea: A CHIPS-funded advance market commitment buys ~1 exabyte over 5 years of byte-addressable working memory from existing >=28-nm U.S. fabs at a fixed $/GB and spec (<=100 ns, >=1e15 endurance or architectural equivalent), open to any revived storage element.
why: Guaranteed demand lets revived elements (pinned wells, T-RAM, MNOS, micro-magnetics) fill idle 200/300-mm trailing capacity now instead of waiting 3-5 years for a DRAM fab; capital intensity and U.S. share.

title: Hitachi single-electron polysilicon memory revived on 130-nm lines
idea: Hitachi's 1990s Yano memory stored a few electrons in a polysilicon nanograin that gated a percolation channel. Reproduce it with 3-nm poly-Si or Si-nanocrystal films on existing 130/90-nm lines, where ~10 stored electrons shift the channel threshold enough to read in a 1T gain structure.
why: Few-electron storage removes the capacitor wall (Fact 1) and the Coulomb-blockade barrier extends retention to seconds or more (Fact 3); the storage grain self-assembles, so old-node litho suffices.

title: Wiegand-wire revival: exchange-spring strips that self-generate read pulses
idea: The Wiegand effect (1970s access cards) uses a hard shell and soft core that snaps abruptly, producing a voltage pulse independent of drive speed. Make planar CoPt-hard/NiFe-soft bilayer strips on an existing 180-nm line; the bit is the hard layer's direction, and a read field ramp triggers a soft-layer snap only when antiparallel, inducing a pulse in a pickup line.
why: Rate-independent, self-generated read signal needs no MTJ fab (sputter plus 180-nm litho); non-volatile and non-destructive because the hard layer is untouched (Facts 3, 8); niche density.
